questions.prompt: Walk through the chain an API request in IDURAR passes from app.js to a generic CRUD controller: what is checked at each step, which mounts skip the chain entirely, what the authentication middleware attaches to the request, and what (if anything) decides whether this caller may touch this particular record.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Mount order is the policy: the auth router (login, reset) is open, the core and ERP API routers sit behind isValidAuthToken, /download and /public are mounted with no auth at all, and the notFound and productionErrors handlers come last.

[w3] isValidAuthToken takes the Bearer value, verifies the JWT signature, loads the Admin and its AdminPassword document (both removed: false) in parallel, demands that this exact token string is present in the stored session array, and only then sets req.admin and calls next().
[w1] Every refusal from that middleware carries jwtExpired: true whatever the real cause (no token, unknown user, revoked session), so the client cannot distinguish them from the flag.
[w2] Entity routes are generated, not hand-written: routerApp registers create/read/update/delete/search/list/listAll/filter/summary for every model in routesList, each wrapped in catchErrors.

[w3] Nothing decides per record: the generic read looks up { _id, removed: false } with no owner condition, and the only role the Admin schema allows is owner, so any authenticated admin can reach any record.
[w2] The role field is a one-value enum defaulting to owner, so there is no second principal to separate; createdBy on invoices records attribution, not access.
[w2] That is acceptable only while the app is single-tenant; once a second user exists, the fix belongs in shared middleware or a base query rather than in each controller.
keyPoints.quote: A per-controller fix is dangerous because one omission is a hole.

questions.prompt: Explain where request data is validated in IDURAR by comparing three requests: creating an invoice, updating a generic entity by id, and listing with query-string filters and a search term. Which layer catches what in each, and what passes straight through to MongoDB?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The invoice create path checks the body against a Joi object schema inside the controller; a Joi object rejects keys it does not declare, so a body carrying extra fields is refused before anything is written, and server-owned fields such as createdBy and paymentStatus are set afterwards.

[w3] The generic update passes the whole req.body to findOneAndUpdate (after forcing removed back to false), so any schema field a client names can be overwritten; only Mongoose's runValidators stands in the way, which checks types and enums, not who may set a field.
[w2] So the depth of validation depends on the entity: invoices, payments and auth get a schema at the boundary, every other model gets only its persistence schema.
keyPoints.quote: Validation rigor is inconsistent across the API.

keyPoints.text: [w2] The list guard refuses an object-valued equal (blocking operator objects smuggled in the value) but uses the filter parameter as a field name unchecked, and sortBy, sortValue and fields are taken raw too.
[w2] The search term q is compiled with new RegExp(q, 'i') without escaping and applied to each requested field, so a caller controls the regular expression the database runs.
[w2] The only path guard is on /public: the decoded sub-path, directory and file are joined under the root and anything resolving outside it is answered 400.
[w1] The Ant Design form rules on the client are a convenience for the user and carry no weight on the server.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict IDURAR's error contract and its one unauthenticated data route: what does a client receive for a Mongoose validation failure, for an unexpected exception, for an unknown URL and for an empty list, and what can an anonymous caller learn or fetch through /download?

keyPoints.text: [w3] catchErrors maps any error named ValidationError to 400 with the fixed message 'Required fields are not supplied', even when the real cause is an enum or cast failure, and attaches the raw error object.

[w3] Every other failure becomes 500 with error.message, the controller name and the serialised error; the production handler likewise returns the error object despite its 'no stacktraces' comment, so internals reach the client.

[w2] The envelope ({ success, result, message }) is consistent, but the status codes are not: an unknown URL is 404 "Api url doesn't exist", a missing record 404 'No document found', and an empty list a 203 with success: true.

[w3] /download has no auth middleware, and its directory segment selects ANY registered Mongoose model by capitalised name; the record is fetched by id with no removed: false filter, so soft-deleted records still render to PDF.
[w2] Its answers also differ by case: an unregistered name returns 404 naming the model, a missing id is thrown as a fake ValidationError, so the route doubles as a model-name oracle.
[w2] The defence offered for it, that ObjectIds are hard to guess, is obscurity, not an access decision.
